Gtk-4.0.gir says "GtkPopoverMenuBar has a single CSS node with name menubar", and a GTK 4.22 process returns `get_css_name()` = 'menubar'. The same mistake appears in four more places. (1) notes.css:77 `notebook.notes-tabs > header > arrow`: GTK 4 puts scroll arrows under `tabs` (`header > tabs > arrow`), and note_pages.rs:486 turns `set_scrollable(true)` on. (2) notes.css:95 `.notes-scroll > viewport`: the scroller wraps a sourceview5::View, which is Scrollable, so no viewport exists (doc.rs:148-163). (3) theme.css:489 `.task-relations expander` matches the *arrow* node of each gtk::Expander (task_pages.rs:915), because GTK 4's tree is `expander-widget > box > title > expander`; and theme.css:490 `expander > title` can never match. (4) theme.css:255/391 use `searchentry`, but GtkSearchEntry's node is `entry` (confirmed in GTK 4.22); these are also counted in the dead-CSS finding.

**Impact.** The Notes window is presented at every launch (app.rs:366 → notes_window.rs:165). Its File/Edit/Search/View bar never gets the intended transparent bar, flat 30px items, 12px/500 secondary text or @wash hover. The desktop GTK theme's `menubar`/`item` rules (padding, accent highlight, any rule line) apply instead, inside Relay's console titlebar. With many open tabs, the notebook scroll arrows also keep the theme's styling. In task details, each disclosure triangle gets 6px of vertical padding instead of the row.

**Fix.** Rename the selectors: `.notes-chrome menubar`, `.notes-chrome menubar > item` (with :hover/:selected), and `notebook.notes-tabs > header > tabs > arrow`. Drop `> viewport` from notes.css:95. Change theme.css:489-490 to `.task-relations expander-widget` and `.task-relations expander-widget > box > title`. Delete the `searchentry` rules.

**Verifier note.** Downgraded to low. The consequence is purely cosmetic: the theme's default menubar item padding and hover apply instead of the flat 30px items, and the notebook arrows and expander padding are unstyled. No behaviour or information is lost. The rename fixes are correct as proposed.

**Also at:** `apps/relay-native/src/css/notes.css:77`, `apps/relay-native/src/css/notes.css:95`, `apps/relay-native/src/theme.css:489`, `apps/relay-native/src/theme.css:490`, `apps/relay-native/src/theme.css:255`, `apps/relay-native/src/note_pages/menu.rs:394`, `apps/relay-native/src/notes_window.rs:40`, `apps/relay-native/src/note_pages.rs:486`, `apps/relay-native/src/task_pages.rs:915`

<a id="ra-533"></a>

#### RA-533 · serve_with_door leaves a stale direct_port when its door fails to bind, so `relay remote pair` links to another instance's door

`crates/relay-cli/src/remote.rs:115` · **low** · Bug · confirmed · effort S

**Problem.** `if let Some(door) = &door { registry.direct_port = Some(door.local_addr.port()); }` (115-117) never clears the field when the door did not open. That happens, for example, when another instance's door already holds 7420, since every instance defaults to that port. `Pair` uses `registry.direct_port.unwrap_or(DEFAULT_PORT)` (227) and prints its 'serve has not run' note only when the field is None (231).

**Impact.** Run the dev engine with --remote while the stable engine owns 7420, then pair for dev. The link points at stable's door, the phone is greeted by the wrong instance, and pairing fails with `pair.invalid` and no hint why.

**Fix.** Set `registry.direct_port = door.as_ref().map(|d| d.local_addr.port())`, and have `pair` warn when no door is recorded for the instance.

**Verifier note.** The practical difference is small. If the field were cleared to None, `pair` would still fall back to DEFAULT_PORT 7420, the same wrong door, and would print a misleading 'relay remote serve has not run' note. The useful fix is to store `door.as_ref().map(|d| d.local_addr.port())` and have `pair` say explicitly that this instance has no open door, possibly because another instance holds the port. Using a different default port per instance would remove the collision altogether.

**Also at:** `crates/relay-cli/src/remote.rs:227`

<a id="ra-534"></a>

#### RA-534 · Bridge keeps the phone connected after the engine side closes

`crates/relay-remote/src/bridge.rs:164` · **low** · Bug · confirmed · effort S

**Problem.** The engine-to-phone pump ends silently on EOF: `while let Ok(Some(line)) = lines.next_line().await { … }` (162-169). `run` meanwhile keeps waiting in `while let Some(line) = inbound.recv().await` (173) while still holding `outbound`. So neither the direct writer nor the tunnel lane closes. The phone learns nothing until it next writes and hits EPIPE.

**Impact.** Run `relay remote serve` beside an engine (MOBILE.md §2), then restart or crash the engine. Every connected phone stays 'connected' to a dead bridge: no events, held-agent notifications or terminal output arrive. Nothing drops, so the reconnect-after-drop the app relies on (MOBILE.md:173) never triggers.

**Fix.** Use `tokio::select!` on the pump's JoinHandle and `inbound.recv()`. When the pump finishes, return, so the transport closes and the phone reconnects.

**Verifier note.** Impact: phones attached through a standalone `relay remote serve` see a dead link for up to one keepalive interval (about 25 s) after the engine restarts, not indefinitely. The fix is unchanged and cheap: `select!` on the pump JoinHandle alongside `inbound.recv()` and return when the pump ends.

**Also at:** `crates/relay-remote/src/bridge.rs:173`, `docs/MOBILE.md:173`

#### RA-535 · /info is readable by any web page (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`) and WebSocket upgrades never check Origin

`crates/relay-remote/src/direct.rs:80` · **low** · Security · confirmed · effort S

**Problem.** The hand-written /info response sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (80). The WebSocket upgrade uses plain `accept_async` (89) with no header callback, so a browser `Origin` is never inspected.

**Impact.** Any site the user visits can `fetch('http://127.0.0.1:7420/info')` (or a LAN address) and read the machine's host name, Relay instance and version, and whether a pairing window is open, which fingerprints the user and machine. It can also open WebSockets to the in-engine door, feeding the DoS above. The native phone app needs neither CORS nor browser-origin sockets.

**Fix.** Drop the CORS header. Use `accept_hdr_async` and refuse upgrades that carry a browser `Origin`.

**Verifier note.** Drop the CORS header and refuse WebSocket upgrades that carry a browser Origin via `accept_hdr_async`. Low impact: information disclosure and a minor contribution to remote#1.

<a id="ra-536"></a>

#### RA-536 · Nagle stays on for every WebSocket socket while each bus line is flushed as its own message

`crates/relay-remote/src/direct.rs:89` · **low** · Performance · confirmed · effort S

**Problem.** Accepted streams go to `accept_async` / `accept_hdr_async` without `set_nodelay(true)` (direct.rs:89, rendezvous.rs:159). The PC dials with `connect_async` (tunnel.rs:57), which tokio-tungstenite runs with `disable_nagle = false`. Every line is then sent with `sink.send(Message::text(line))`, a feed plus a flush per line (direct.rs:98, rendezvous.rs:188 and 263, tunnel.rs:67).

**Impact.** Back-to-back small lines (a response followed by its echo frame or event) leave the second one waiting for the peer's delayed ACK, about 40 ms on Linux/Android. That wait is paid on every hop, so twice through the rendezvous, and shows up as lag in terminal echo and responses on the phone. Not measured.

**Fix.** Call `set_nodelay(true)` on accepted streams and dial with `connect_async_with_config(url, None, true)`. Batch with `feed` while the queue is non-empty and `flush` once, as relay-core's socket writer already does.

**Verifier note.** The extra latency of up to ~40 ms per hop is inferred from TCP behaviour, not observed. Minimal fix: `stream.set_nodelay(true)` before both accepts, and `connect_async_with_config(url, None, true)` in tunnel.rs. Batching (feed while the channel has more, then one flush) is optional on top of that.

**Also at:** `crates/relay-remote/src/rendezvous.rs:159`, `crates/relay-remote/src/tunnel.rs:57`

<a id="ra-537"></a>

#### RA-537 · Phone-supplied device names keep control characters and are printed raw by `relay remote devices`

`crates/relay-remote/src/registry.rs:220` · **low** · Security · confirmed · effort S

**Problem.** `name: if name.is_empty() { … } else { name.chars().take(64).collect() }` (220) trims `hello.device_name` but keeps ESC and other control characters. relay-cli remote.rs:245 prints `d.name` straight to the terminal.

**Impact.** Whoever pairs (anyone who saw the code) can choose a name containing terminal escape sequences, such as OSC 52 clipboard writes, title changes, or cursor moves that hide or forge rows. They fire whenever the user lists devices.

**Fix.** Filter `char::is_control` (and optionally bidi override characters) when storing the name.

**Verifier note.** The only meaningful trigger is a device that was legitimately paired, or one paired with a stolen code; the latter is already a much worse compromise. The fix is as proposed: filter `char::is_control` (and optionally bidi overrides) in redeem, or escape on output in the CLI.

<a id="ra-538"></a>

#### RA-538 · Room secret travels in the host URL's query string

`crates/relay-remote/src/tunnel.rs:19` · **low** · Security · confirmed · effort S

**Problem.** `format!("{}/host/{}?secret={}", r.url, r.room, r.secret)` (19). The server reads the secret from the query (rendezvous.rs:98-102).

**Impact.** TLS proxies in front of the rendezvous log request URIs with their query strings (nginx's default access log; Caddy when logging is enabled), so the secret is written to disk on the VPS on every reconnect. Over ws:// it is visible to everyone on the path. With it, anyone can host the room, evicting the PC, and phones then talk to an impostor that sees whatever they send.

**Fix.** Send the secret in a request header (e.g. `Authorization: Bearer …`, read in the `accept_hdr_async` callback) or as the first frame after the upgrade, so it never appears in a URL.

**Verifier note.** Over ws://, which relay-cli remote.rs:280-284 allows with a warning, a request header is just as visible on the wire. So the fix only helps with proxy and access-log exposure, not with ws://. The fix is to send the secret in a header read in the accept_hdr_async callback, or as the first frame after the upgrade.

**Also at:** `crates/relay-remote/src/rendezvous.rs:99`, `crates/relay-remote/src/rendezvous.rs:98`, `crates/relay-cli/src/remote.rs:43`, `crates/relay-cli/src/remote.rs:283`, `docs/MOBILE.md:87`

<a id="ra-539"></a>

#### RA-539 · Tunnel dial has no timeout, and the backoff never resets after a long successful connection

`crates/relay-remote/src/tunnel.rs:57` · **low** · Error handling · confirmed · effort S

**Problem.** `tokio_tungstenite::connect_async(url.as_str()).await` (57) has no timeout around the TCP, TLS and HTTP-upgrade steps. `spawn` resets `backoff` only when `connect_once` returns Ok (34-36). Connections normally end in Err (a socket error, or the 90 s silence bail), so after hours connected the redial still waits at whatever level the backoff had reached, up to 30 s.

**Impact.** A dial that stalls after the TCP handshake hangs, with nothing logged, until TCP gives up (~15 min), or forever if the peer accepted and never answers. Examples: the laptop suspends mid-dial, or a proxy accepts and never responds. Phones are told the PC is offline the whole time. This defeats the liveness work the 30 s ping and 90 s silence limit were added for.

**Fix.** Wrap the dial in `tokio::time::timeout` (~15 s). Reset `backoff` once `connect_async` succeeds, e.g. by having `connect_once` report 'connected' separately from how the connection ended.

**Verifier note.** The no-reset bug costs at most 30 s of extra reconnect delay. The missing timeout matters only in rare stalled-handshake cases. A dial to a host that is down fails on the OS SYN timeout, about 2 min. Fix: wrap the dial in `tokio::time::timeout`, and reset backoff once the dial succeeds.

**Also at:** `crates/relay-remote/src/tunnel.rs:34`, `crates/relay-remote/src/tunnel.rs:29`

**Merged duplicates:** sec-remote-door#14

<a id="ra-540"></a>

#### RA-540 · Actor gate is bypassed by a frame containing several lines

`crates/relay-remote/src/wire.rs:96` · **low** · Security · confirmed · effort S

**Problem.** `gate` parses the whole WebSocket frame: `let Ok(value) = serde_json::from_str::<serde_json::Value>(line) else { return Gate::Forward; };` (96-98). A frame of two JSON objects separated by a newline fails with trailing characters, so it is forwarded verbatim (bridge.rs:177-181). The engine reads it with `lines()` (relay-core socket.rs:323, 335) as separate requests, and the second one was never gated. The comment at 92-94 is also wrong: valid non-object JSON is rejected, not forwarded.

**Impact.** This breaks the guarantee stated in MOBILE.md:180-182 and ARCHITECTURE.md:61-62: 'every line a phone sends is gated to actor `user`' and 'a phone cannot borrow an agent's identity even with a guessed token'. The engine still refuses `system`, refuses `test` on stable, and requires a session token. But a phone that has seen an agent's RELAY_TOKEN (e.g. in that agent's terminal) can act as that agent, and its actions are audited as the agent's.

**Fix.** Split each frame on newline and gate and forward every non-empty piece separately, or refuse frames that contain a newline. While there, parse only a small borrowed head struct (`actor`, `id`) instead of building a full `Value` tree for every line.

**Verifier note.** Only an already-paired, authenticated device can trigger this, and it gains no privilege beyond the user it already acts as. Fix: refuse frames that contain '\n', or split them and gate each piece.

**Also at:** `crates/relay-remote/src/bridge.rs:177`, `docs/MOBILE.md:180`, `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:61`, `crates/relay-remote/src/bridge.rs:202`, `crates/relay-remote/src/direct.rs:107`, `crates/relay-core/src/socket.rs:335`, `crates/relay-remote/src/tunnel.rs:139`

**Merged duplicates:** lens-docs#16, sec-remote-door#11

<a id="ra-541"></a>

#### RA-541 · A phone credential carries the whole `user` bus (every op in the 220-op catalogue) instead of the roughly 30 ops the phone uses

`crates/relay-remote/src/wire.rs:100` · **low** · Security · confirmed · effort M

**Problem.** The door's only filter is the actor check at wire.rs:99-100: `let allowed = actor == "user" || (actor == "test" && instance.accepts_test_actor());`. lib.rs:13-14 says the bridge 'forwards bus lines to the socket door as actor `user`'. On the socket door `user` has no scope: engine.rs:1355 `(Actor::User, _) | (Actor::Test, _) => Ok(None)` means the role and scope guardrail layer (engine.rs:870 `if let Some(sid) = session_id`) never runs, and every UserOnly op is admitted (relay-bus registry.rs:59-63, envelope.rs:37-40). That trust model was written for local callers with the same uid: BUS.md:1119-1121 says 'Same uid = same trust (§0.6) ... No RPC over the network. Unix socket only.' A phone can therefore call settings.set, including `providers.claude.path` and `device.adb_path`, which choose the executables the engine runs (providers.rs:271-280, handlers/device.rs:550-560). It can also call guardrail.config.set, guardrail.grant.revoke, file.write/delete, project.add/remove, worktree.remove, git.push, app.quit, skill.install, plugin.enable and github.connect. MOBILE.md:144-169 lists what the app actually uses: session.*, task.*, mailbox.send, guardrail.confirm/reject, git.status/diff and notify.*.

**Impact.** Each other weakness in the door turns straight into arbitrary code execution as the user: a token sniffed at pairing, MITM or rendezvous injection, a revoke that leaves the live link up, or a code redeemed by someone who saw the QR. For example, an attacker can point `providers.claude.path` at another binary, or relax the guardrail config, then start a session. Audit rows also cannot tell phone actions from keyboard actions. MOBILE.md:195 accepts that 'a paired phone is you', but nothing the phone does needs to reconfigure executables or guardrails.

**Fix.** Filter by op as well as by actor. Add an explicit allow-list in wire::gate of the ops the app sends, after fixing the newline-framing bypass. Refuse settings, guardrail.config, provider, plugin, skill, file, worktree, app.quit and similar ops. Better: give remote connections their own actor (for example `remote:<device>`) with an engine-side allowlist layer and their own audit attribution.

**Verifier note.** Severity drops from medium to low. An allow-list would not prevent code execution from a compromised phone credential. What it would buy is narrower: (1) the phone could not make persistent reconfigurations that outlive a `relay remote revoke`, such as providers.*.path, device.adb_path, guardrail.config.set or plugin/skill install; (2) phone actions could be told apart in the audit, given a distinct actor such as remote:<device>. Implement it only after the newline-framing bypass (#11) is fixed, and update MOBILE.md §5/§6, which currently promise the full user bus.

**Also at:** `crates/relay-remote/src/lib.rs:13`, `crates/relay-core/src/engine.rs:1355`, `crates/relay-core/src/engine.rs:870`, `crates/relay-bus/src/registry.rs:59`, `crates/relay-core/src/providers.rs:271`, `crates/relay-core/src/handlers/device.rs:550`, `docs/engine/BUS.md:1119`, `docs/MOBILE.md:195`

#### RA-542 · Modeling recipe make_lods creates LODs as siblings, so blender_export with `objects` drops them

`plugins/blender/skills/blender-modeling/reference/modeling-recipes.md:199` · **low** · Bug · confirmed · effort S

<a id="ra-543"></a>

#### RA-543 · Nothing scans dependencies for advisories, and Cargo.lock currently carries a RustSec-flagged crate

`.github/workflows/ci.yml:38` · **low** · Security · confirmed · effort S

**Problem.** CI runs only `cargo test --locked` and clippy (37-41). There is no cargo-audit or cargo-deny job, no deny.toml and no Dependabot config. Cargo.lock pins `faster-hex` 0.10.0 (Cargo.lock:577-578), which RUSTSEC-2026-0306 flags (AVX2 read past the source buffer in `hex_decode_unchecked`, patched in ≥0.10.1). gix reaches it only through the checked `hex_decode`, which requires `src.len() >= 2*dst.len()`, so it is not exploitable here, but nothing reported it. I checked every 2026 RustSec advisory: the locked versions of rustls (0.23.45), rustls-webpki (0.103.15), event-listener, memmap2, anyhow, rand and bytes are already patched. All dependencies come from crates.io, with no git or wildcard sources.

**Impact.** The next advisory against a crate on the network-facing phone door (tungstenite, rustls) or the repository-parsing path (gix, tree-sitter) will go unnoticed. `--locked` keeps the vulnerable version until someone bumps it by hand.

**Fix.** Add a PR and scheduled `cargo deny check advisories bans sources` job (or `cargo audit`), with a deny.toml that refuses git and unknown registries. Enable Dependabot for cargo and github-actions. Run `cargo update -p faster-hex`.

**Verifier note.** I did not verify the exact patched version (>=0.10.1) or the claim that gix uses only the checked path; I checked only that the advisory exists. Fix as proposed: a scheduled `cargo deny check advisories` or `cargo audit` job, plus Dependabot.

**Also at:** `Cargo.lock:577`

<a id="ra-544"></a>

#### RA-544 · CI actions are pinned to mutable tags or a branch, and the mobile-apk job exposes a write token and the signing secrets to every step and third-party action

`.github/workflows/mobile-apk.yml:38` · **low** · Security · confirmed · effort S

**Problem.** `permissions: contents: write` is set for the whole workflow (37-38). `actions/checkout@v4` (68) keeps the token in .git/config by default. `npm ci` (111-112), which runs dependency install scripts, `npx expo prebuild` and the Gradle/CMake build (166-173) all run while it is readable. The keystore and passwords are written to `android/app/release.keystore` and `android/gradle.properties` (117-131) and stay there for later steps and for the post-job hooks of `gradle/actions/setup-gradle@v4` (101) and `hendrikmuhs/ccache-action@v1.2` (106). The release upload uses `softprops/action-gh-release@v2` (198). Every action is referenced by tag. ci.yml uses `dtolnay/rust-toolchain@master`, a branch (28), and `Swatinem/rust-cache@v2` (33), and has no `permissions:` block. deploy/rendezvous.Dockerfile uses unpinned `rust:1.94-bookworm` and `debian:bookworm-slim` (46, 54).

**Impact.** A compromised npm or Gradle dependency, or a re-pointed action tag (as in the tj-actions/changed-files incident of March 2025), running in mobile-apk could push commits, tags and releases with the write token. It could also take the Android release keystore and passwords, enabling signed malicious updates of the phone app that controls the PC. Any push to dtolnay/rust-toolchain's master branch runs in every engine CI job.

**Fix.** Set `permissions: contents: read` at workflow level and grant `contents: write` only to a separate release job that downloads the built artifact. Set `persist-credentials: false` on checkout. Pin every action to a full commit SHA (Dependabot can keep them current). Materialize signing files only in the Gradle step and delete them afterwards. Pin Docker base images by digest.

**Verifier note.** The Dockerfile lines are deploy/rendezvous.Dockerfile:9 and :17, not 46/54. 'Materialize signing files only in the Gradle step' does little against a compromised Gradle or npm-native dependency, because signing needs the key inside that same Gradle process. The parts that help: least privilege (a read-only token by default, with `contents: write` only in a separate release job that uploads the downloaded artifact), `persist-credentials: false`, and SHA-pinned actions. This workflow builds the out-of-scope phone app, but the finding concerns repository token scope, so it stays.

**Also at:** `.github/workflows/ci.yml:28`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml:33`, `.github/workflows/mobile-apk.yml:68`, `.github/workflows/mobile-apk.yml:117`, `.github/workflows/mobile-apk.yml:198`, `deploy/rendezvous.Dockerfile:46`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml:11-13`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml:23`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml:50`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml:52`

**Merged duplicates:** scripts-infra#10

<a id="ra-545"></a>

#### RA-545 · Workspace dependency choices compile avoidable crates: rand 0.9 beside tungstenite's rand 0.10, and gix with its full default feature set

`Cargo.toml:32` · **low** · Performance · confirmed · effort S

**Problem.** Cargo.toml:32 declares `rand = "0.9"`. Cargo.lock has rand 0.9.5 (pulled by relay-core and relay-remote) and rand 0.10.3 (pulled by tungstenite 0.30.0), so rand, rand_core and getrandom are each built twice (getrandom 0.3.4 is reached only through rand_core 0.9.5), plus rand_chacha 0.9. Cargo.toml:35 declares `gix = { version = "0.86", features = ["status", "worktree-mutation", "revision"] }` with default features left on. gix 0.86's defaults ('basic' + 'extras') already include those three features. They also pull gix-blame, gix-archive, gix-worktree-stream, gix-mailmap, gix-credentials, gix-prompt and gix-negotiate (all present in Cargo.lock), none of which relay-core calls. Its gix uses are open, status/is_dirty, rev_parse_single, tree diff and remote_tracking_ref_name.

**Impact.** Clean builds take longer for code that never runs, and the cost recurs in every checkout or worktree that builds its own target/.

**Fix.** Use `rand = "0.10"`. It has 5 call sites; RngCore becomes Rng at relay-remote/src/registry.rs:8 and relay-core/src/sessions.rs:92. Use `gix = { version = "0.86", default-features = false, features = ["status", "worktree-mutation", "revision", "sha1", "max-performance-safe"] }` and add back only what the compiler asks for (this audit could not compile to confirm the minimal set).

**Verifier note.** In rand 0.10 the trait renames (RngCore and Rng) change the imports at relay-remote/src/registry.rs:8 and relay-core/src/sessions.rs:92 (`fill_bytes`). sessions.rs:75 also uses `rand::seq::IndexedRandom`, so check that import too. The minimal gix feature set must be found by compiling: `status` brings in dirwalk, attributes and index on its own, so the savings are mainly blame, archive, worktree-stream, mailmap and credentials.

Every session that engine launches then runs hooks and the MCP server from the parent engine's relay (the main checkout's build), not the worktree build under test, so hook and MCP changes look verified without ever having run.

**Fix.** Next to line 12, add `unset RELAY_SESSION RELAY_TOKEN RELAY_BRIEF RELAY_STORE RELAY_WORKTREE RELAY_PROJECT RELAY_BIN` (or use `env -u ...` for the serve command only).

**Verifier note.** The only variable with a proven effect is RELAY_BIN. RELAY_SESSION/RELAY_TOKEN/RELAY_STORE/RELAY_WORKTREE/RELAY_BRIEF/RELAY_PROJECT leak too but do no demonstrated harm here. Unsetting them is still good hygiene, because the engine's children and any CLI call without --actor would act as the agent. The fix in the finding is right: unset them all next to line 12.

#### RA-547 · Launcher failures are invisible when Relay is started from the desktop entry, and a failed build makes Relay impossible to open

`run.sh:20` · **low** · Error handling · confirmed · effort S

**Problem.** The installed entry runs run.sh with `Terminal=false` (apps/relay-native/resources/com.quietsoftware.Relay4.desktop:8; the installed copy in ~/.local/share/applications was confirmed). run.sh reports progress and failures only on stdout and stderr: 'Building Relay...' (16), the build log on failure (20-23), and 'Relay engine did not become ready' plus a log tail (37-38). A failed `cargo build` exits even when a previously working target/debug/relay-native exists. relay-native is not compiled in CI (ci.yml:69-82), so a commit that breaks only the native client can reach main.

**Impact.** After pulling a change that breaks the build, or with a half-edited main checkout, clicking the Relay icon does nothing: no window, no message, and the error lands only in the journal. A cold build after a dependency change runs for minutes with no feedback, which invites repeated clicks that queue parallel launches.

**Fix.** When stderr is not a terminal (`[[ -t 2 ]]`), report failures with notify-send or zenity, including the last lines of the log, and show a 'Building Relay...' notification. Consider offering the last good build, with a visible warning, when the build fails and target/debug/relay-native exists. Add StartupNotify=true to the template.

**Verifier note.** Downgrade to low: it is a usability gap in a source-checkout launcher, not a failure in a core flow. The claim that 'repeated clicks queue parallel launches' is weak. Concurrent cargo builds serialize on the target-dir lock, and the GTK application id makes a later client register against the first. A notify-send fallback when `! [[ -t 2 ]]` is a reasonable, cheap fix. Falling back to the last good build is a product choice and does not fix a bug.

**Also at:** `run.sh:16`, `run.sh:37-38`, `apps/relay-native/resources/com.quietsoftware.Relay4.desktop:8`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml:69-82`

#### RA-548 · install-native-desktop.py escapes Exec only for the quoting layer, so checkout paths containing $, a double quote or a backtick produce an entry GLib rejects

`scripts/install-native-desktop.py:19` · **low** · Bug · confirmed · effort S

**Problem.** Lines 18-20 prefix each of backslash, double quote, backtick and dollar with one backslash. The Desktop Entry spec applies the string-value escape before the quoting rule, so a literal $ inside a quoted argument must be written as two backslashes followed by $. I checked this against GLib 2.88 (PyGObject GLib.KeyFile plus g_shell_parse_argv). For /home/a/$HOME/run.sh, /home/a/say "hi"/run.sh and a path containing backticks, the generated line makes get_string fail with 'Key file contains key "Exec" which has a value that cannot be interpreted'. The comment at 16-17 claims such paths are handled. Line 22 `desktop.replace("Exec=relay-native", ...)` also does nothing, silently, if the template line changes, and would also rewrite a future TryExec=relay-native line.

**Impact.** A checkout under such a path gets a launcher entry that GLib-based menus cannot read or launch.

**Fix.** After the quoting-level escapes, add `argument = argument.replace('\\', '\\\\')`, which doubles every backslash. With this, all five test paths round-trip through GLib to the original argv[0]. Replace the substring edit with a line-anchored one that fails loudly unless ^Exec=relay-native$ occurs exactly once.

**Verifier note.** The trigger is rare: the checkout path has to contain $, " or a backtick. The broken entry is only a menu launcher, and ./run.sh still works. The fix is right: double every backslash after the quoting-level escapes. The line-22 fragility is a secondary note, not a current bug.

#### RA-549 · Server-to-client envelope types reject unknown fields, so any additive envelope change disconnects older clients

`crates/relay-bus/src/envelope.rs:148` · **low** · Bug · plausible · effort S

**Problem.** `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` is on Response (148), Event (218), Frame (258), MailHint (141), BusError (error.rs:48) and Confirm (error.rs:41). BUS.md §12 says additive changes do not bump `v` and that clients ignore unknown fields, and the `mail` sideband was added exactly that way. The GTK reader parses each line strictly, and any error ends the connection and fails all pending replies (apps/relay-native/src/client.rs:233-250 → Error::Protocol). `relay_core::socket::Client::next`, used by the CLI, MCP and hooks, is just as strict (socket.rs:785-797).

**Impact.** After any optional field is added to Response, Event, Frame or BusError, a client from the previous build disconnects on the first line that carries it. Mixed builds are normal in this workflow: run.sh keeps an already-running engine across rebuilds and the window can outlive an engine restart.

**Fix.** Keep deny_unknown_fields on Request and on payloads only. Remove it from the server-to-client types: Response, Event, Frame, BusError, Confirm and MailHint.

**Verifier note.** Latent compatibility hazard, not a current failure. The fix is as proposed: remove deny_unknown_fields from the server-to-client types (Response, Event, Frame, MailHint, BusError, Confirm) and keep it on Request and payloads. The run.sh case cited in the finding is the safe direction, because a newer client reading an older engine never sees unknown fields.

**Why only plausible.** The mechanism is real. Response, Event, Frame and MailHint (envelope.rs:141,148,218,258) and BusError/Confirm (error.rs) are #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]. The native reader parses each line into these types and turns any parse error into Error::Protocol, which ends the reader loop and fails every pending reply (apps/relay-native/src/client.rs:233-257). relay_core::socket::Client::next (socket.rs:785-797) is just as strict. This contradicts the crate's own rule: the result! macro (ops/mod.rs:15) is deliberately lenient because 'clients ignore unknown fields, §12', and the `mail` sideband was added to Response as an additive change. The trigger has two parts: a future additive envelope field, and an older reader talking to a newer engine. Examples of such readers: a long-lived `relay mcp` process of an agent session that started before a rebuild and engine restart, or the window reconnecting to a restarted engine. run.sh's normal path (old engine, new window) is the safe direction, so the skew needs an engine restart. Nothing breaks at this commit.

**Also at:** `crates/relay-bus/src/error.rs:48`, `apps/relay-native/src/client.rs:247`, `crates/relay-core/src/socket.rs:790`

#### RA-550 · ue_setup_check fix commits remote Python, console commands and any-function calls, unauthenticated, into the shared Config/DefaultRemoteControl.ini

`crates/relay-cli/src/unreal.rs:675` · **low** · Security · plausible · effort M

**Problem.** RC_KEYS sets bAutoStartWebServer, bEnableRemotePythonExecution, bAllowConsoleCommandRemoteExecution and bAllowAnyRemoteFunctionCall all to "True" (675-680). They are merged into `project.root.join("Config/DefaultRemoteControl.ini")` (705-710), a project config that is normally committed, by a tool any agent can call (setup_check, 1461). launch() also always passes -RCWebControlEnable (unreal_process.rs:295). Nothing writes a passphrase, an origin restriction or a bind address. The plugin's security note says only to keep the port on localhost (plugins/unreal-engine/docs/setup.md:52-55).

**Impact.** Once an agent has run the fix and the config is committed, every teammate's editor auto-starts an HTTP endpoint on 127.0.0.1:30010 that runs arbitrary Python as that developer. The teammates never opted in. TCP localhost is reachable from every local account on a shared machine. Web pages may also reach it through DNS rebinding or permissive CORS, depending on how Remote Control handles Origin and Host headers, which cannot be checked from this repository.

**Fix.** Write these keys to the per-user Saved/Config/<Platform>Editor/RemoteControl.ini, or require explicit human confirmation before touching Default*.ini. Also turn on the engine's access restrictions (restricted origin, passphrase) and send UE_REMOTE_CONTROL_PASSPHRASE. Explain the exposure in the setup advice.

**Verifier note.** UE_REMOTE_CONTROL_PASSPHRASE is already sent as a `Passphrase` header when it is set (remote_at, around line 1812, and setup.md lists it), so that part of the fix exists. A better fix is to write the keys to the per-user Saved/Config/<Platform>Editor/ ini, or to state explicitly in the advice that Config/DefaultRemoteControl.ini is shared and should not be committed without the team's agreement. Restricting origins is optional hardening. Drop the console-command and any-function keys unless a tool needs them.

**Why only plausible.** The facts are correct. RC_KEYS (675-680) enables auto-start, remote Python, console commands and any-function calls. write_remote_control_ini merges them into project.root/Config/DefaultRemoteControl.ini (705-710), a project config that UE projects normally commit. It is reached from ue_setup_check fix=true (1461), which an agent can call. Nothing configures origin restrictions or a passphrase. However, remote Python on localhost is the bridge's whole purpose, and setup.md documents and accepts it ("The Remote Control server can run arbitrary editor Python. Keep it bound to localhost"). The advice string at 1487 tells the agent exactly what was written. With remote Python already on, the console-command and any-function keys add no capability. What remains is the scope: writing to the shared Default*.ini turns the server on for anyone who later pulls the commit, without their opting in. The browser/DNS-rebinding route depends on Remote Control's CORS and Host handling, which cannot be established from this repository. On the single-user desktop this app targets, the exposure is the user's own documented choice.

#### RA-551 · ue_run_tests' filter check misses ',' (which -ExecCmds splits on) and the headless run passes no -TestExit, so it can hang until the timeout and lose all output

`crates/relay-cli/src/unreal.rs:1079` · **low** · Bug · plausible · effort S

**Problem.** The check is `anyhow::ensure!(!filter.contains(';') && !filter.contains('"'), ...)` (1079), and the command is built as `.arg(format!("-ExecCmds=Automation RunTests {filter};Quit"))` (1105). The plugin's own reference documents -ExecCmds as comma-separated (`-ExecCmds="cmd1,cmd2"`, plugins/unreal-engine/skills/unreal-performance/reference/console-commands.md:4,68) and recommends -TestExit (skills/unreal-build-packaging/reference/uat-commands.md:123). On timeout, output_with_timeout returns Ok(None), so `.ok_or_else(...)?` (1109-1110) throws stdout away, and the report dir created at 1100-1101 is removed only on the success path (1129).

**Impact.** A filter such as "MyGame.A,MyGame.B" becomes two commands, "Automation RunTests MyGame.A" and "MyGame.B;Quit", so the Quit never reaches the automation handler. The editor process then idles until timeout_s (1800 s by default), and the agent gets 'did not finish within its timeout' with no test output. Each timeout also leaves a Saved/Relay/TestReport/<uuid> folder behind.

**Fix.** Reject ',' or translate it to '+', the RunTests separator. Add -TestExit="Automation Test Queue Empty". Remove the report dir on every path, and return the partial stdout on timeout (this needs output_with_timeout to hand it back).

**Verifier note.** The leaked report dir on any error or timeout path is certain. The comma split depends on UE's ExecCmds parsing. Cheapest fix: reject ',' in the guard (or map it to '+'), add -TestExit="Automation Test Queue Empty" as a backstop, and remove the report dir on every exit path.

**Why only plausible.** The guard at 1079 rejects only ';' and '"'. The headless command is `-ExecCmds=Automation RunTests {filter};Quit` (1105) and adds no -TestExit, although the repo's own skill references add -TestExit (uat-commands.md:123, unreal-testing-debugging/SKILL.md:100). The same references describe -ExecCmds as comma-separated (console-commands.md:4,68). If UE splits ExecCmds on ',', which matches its documented behavior but I could not check against engine source here, a filter like "A,B" leaves "B;Quit" as an unknown command, so Quit never runs. The headless editor then idles until timeout_s (1800 s by default). On timeout, output_with_timeout returns Ok(None), and `.ok_or_else(...)?` (1109-1110) drops all stdout. The early return also skips the report-dir cleanup at 1129, which leaves Saved/Relay/TestReport/<uuid> behind. The trigger requires an agent to pass a comma in a field the schema describes as a single 'test path prefix', so it is uncommon.

**Also at:** `crates/relay-cli/src/unreal.rs:1100-1131`

`crates/relay-cli/src/unreal_py/common.py:191` · **low** · Error handling · plausible · effort S

When get_ref_pose_transform is missing, the Skeleton fallback (lines 178-182) drops every reference-pose rotation without a warning.

The get_ref_pose_transform fallback (common.py:181-182) only matters on engine versions without that UFUNCTION, which recent UE versions have, so it is a minor aside. Severity is low because the cause is a misused parameter and a hint is visible. Fix: check `isinstance(anim, unreal.AnimSequenceBase)` up front (or reject length 0), and count the bones that fell back and add a problem when any did.

A BlendSpace is not an AnimSequenceBase, so the Python binding should raise TypeError on every bone and the tool would silently measure the reference pose. I could not confirm the engine's behaviour from here: whether UE raises or just logs for a montage, an AnimSequence from another skeleton, or a missing bone track. Without that, the only trigger I can stand behind is an agent passing the wrong asset type. That is a misuse of a parameter documented as 'Animation sequence path'.

#### RA-553 · Broken imports are deleted with a path function the code documents as failing after a failed import, and Rust then says they were deleted

`crates/relay-cli/src/unreal_py/import_fbx.py:111` · **low** · Error handling · plausible · effort M

**Problem.** `ok = unreal.EditorAssetLibrary.delete_asset(package)`, with exceptions swallowed. common.py:28-30 and D162 note that EditorAssetLibrary's path functions (does_asset_exist, save_asset, delete_asset) 'were seen returning False for every asset for the rest of a session after a failed import'. The import task has already saved the assets (line 55, `save=True`). blender.rs:428-432 tells the agent 'the broken assets were deleted again' whenever the import failed, without reading the per-path `deleted` flags.

**Impact.** In exactly the failure this cleanup exists for, broken assets (empty meshes, transient materials) can stay saved in Content/ while the agent is told they were deleted.

**Fix.** Delete by object (`EditorAssetLibrary.delete_loaded_asset(unreal.load_asset(p))`, or AssetTools/ObjectTools), confirm the deletion through the registry (`asset_exists`), and have Rust report every path whose `deleted` is false.

**Verifier note.** Leftover broken assets need both importers to fail and delete_asset to misbehave, and the deleted:false flags are already in the returned text. Fix: have compare() read attempts[-1].cleaned_up and name the paths whose deleted is false. Optionally confirm each delete with asset_exists() (registry-based), or delete by loaded object.

**Why only plausible.** remove() (import_fbx.py:105-115) calls EditorAssetLibrary.delete_asset and swallows exceptions. common.py:28-30 and D162 (DECISIONS.md:962-963) record that this library's path functions, delete_asset by name, returned False for a whole session after a failed import, and asset_exists() was added to work around it. The import task saves with save=True (line 55), so a delete that silently fails leaves the broken assets on disk. compare() at blender.rs:428-432 always says 'the broken assets were deleted again' when failed is true. However, that message also embeds the full attempts JSON, which includes each path's `deleted: false`, so the agent is not left with only the false claim. A retry with replace_existing also overwrites a leftover from the first attempt. Leftovers therefore stay only when every importer fails and delete_asset also misbehaves. I could not establish that the empty-mesh or transient-material outcome counts as the 'failed import' that triggered the documented EditorAssetLibrary breakage.

#### RA-554 · On connect, device.watch is awaited before the notice loop starts draining, so 64 queued events block its reply

`apps/relay-native/src/app.rs:1166` · **low** · Concurrency · plausible · effort S

**Problem.** `if *ui.page.borrow() == "devices" { let _ = ui.call("device.watch", json!({"on":true})).await; }` runs after bus.subscribe has succeeded but before `while let Ok(notice) = notices.recv().await` (app.rs:1165-1170). The reader pushes events with `reader_notices.send(Notice::Event(event)).await` into a 64-slot channel (client.rs:179, 235-238) and reads no further lines while that send waits. The device.watch response behind the 65th event is therefore never read.

**Impact.** Reconnecting while on the Devices page during an event burst (for example several agents editing files; file.changed is debounced only per worktree, watch.rs:120) stalls every request on the control connection until device.watch times out after 30 s.

**Fix.** Spawn the device.watch call as its own future, as navigate() already does (app.rs:1339-1347), and enter the drain loop immediately.

**Verifier note.** I could not show that more than 64 subscribed events realistically arrive in the few milliseconds between the subscribe reply and the device.watch reply. That needs a heavy event burst at the moment of a manual reconnect while the Devices page is shown (at startup the page is not Devices, so it applies only to Reconnect). It recovers after the 30 s timeout. Fix as proposed: spawn the device.watch call instead of awaiting it before the drain loop.

**Why only plausible.** The mechanism is real. On reconnect while the Devices page is open, `ui.call("device.watch", ...).await` (app.rs:1165-1167) runs before the `notices.recv()` drain loop starts. The client's reader task sends each Event into a 64-slot bounded channel with `.send(...).await` (client.rs:181, 235-238) and reads no further socket lines while that send is pending. If more than 64 events arrive before the device.watch response, the response is never read, the call times out after 30 s, and every other response on that connection, including the refresh() calls just fired, is stuck behind it. navigate() already spawns device.watch as a separate future (app.rs:1339-1347).

#### RA-555 · Approval prompts show agent-chosen commands and paths without neutralising bidi or invisible characters

`apps/relay-native/src/guardrail_pages.rs:427` · **low** · Security · plausible · effort S

**Problem.** `card.append(&mono(value))` goes through `paragraph()` to `gtk::Label::new(Some(text))`. Pango applies the Unicode bidi algorithm to label text, honouring U+202A–U+202E and U+2066–U+2069, and renders zero-width and format characters (U+200B–U+200D, U+2060, U+FEFF) as nothing. Nothing rejects or escapes them: `grants::validate` checks only emptiness and `..`. The exact-action view uses `serde_json::to_string_pretty` (333), which escapes only `"`, `\` and C0 controls, so U+202E passes through raw there as well. The engine relies on the person reading the value exactly: `covers_command` matches the grant's words literally, and "a grant ending in a lone `*` covers everything that starts with the words before it, and the person approving it reads that `*`" (grants.rs:137-149).

**Impact.** A prompt-injected agent can request an exception whose displayed command or path reads differently from the bytes that will be granted (Trojan-Source-style reordering, or look-alike values containing invisible characters). The user approves what they see, and the grant lets the logical command past the denied-commands rule.

**Fix.** Route every agent-supplied string through one display helper. It should replace bidi controls, zero-width and format characters, and non-newline controls with visible, highlighted escapes, and flag the card "contains hidden characters". Also reject such characters for `command` values in `grants::validate`.

**Verifier note.** Downgrade to low and treat it as hardening: escape or flag bidi, format and zero-width characters in agent-supplied values before display, and reject them in grants::validate for command values. A related and more consequential problem showed up while verifying this, and should be checked separately: command_words drops quoted words (`filter(|word| !word.quoted)`) on both the grant and the run command. A command grant therefore does not bind its quoted arguments, which the person approving it does read.

**Why only plausible.** The missing neutralisation is real. Values reach `gtk::Label` through paragraph/mono (guardrail_pages.rs:24-36, 427), `grants::validate` (grants.rs:195-216) checks only emptiness, `..` and cap syntax, and Pango applies bidi to label text. The claimed exploit is much weaker than stated, though. Bidi controls cannot hide characters; they only reorder them. Any control character placed in a command becomes literal bytes in a shell word: `command_words` (guardrail.rs:1001-1008) splits on shell syntax, so `‮target` is a different filename, not `target`. A display that looks harmless while the bytes are harmful therefore needs the controls to stand as separate words that reorder whole arguments, which only matters for order-sensitive commands such as cp, mv or ln. Zero-width characters change bytes but do not make a command more dangerous. I could not build a convincing case where the approved display reads benign and the granted command is destructive. The agent can also simply ask for a dangerous command openly. What remains is defense-in-depth hardening.

**Also at:** `apps/relay-native/src/guardrail_pages.rs:333`, `apps/relay-native/src/guardrail_pages.rs:260`, `apps/relay-native/src/guardrail_pages.rs:805`, `crates/relay-core/src/guardrail/grants.rs:137`, `crates/relay-core/src/guardrail/grants.rs:195`

`apps/relay-native/src/guardrail_pages.rs:582` · **low** · Security · plausible · effort S

**Problem.** show_prompt appends the slot without any gating, and its tick callback reveals it on the next frame (605-614). **Verifier note.** Arming the keys about 300-500 ms after child-revealed, and naming the session and value in the confirmation notice, are reasonable cheap hardening. This is not a guardrail bypass, and it should not rate above low.

**Why only plausible.** The mechanism is accurate. show_prompt appends the slot (582), and the tick callback reveals it on the next frame (605-614), with no arming delay. The Approve keys (445-446) are sensitive and targetable once they are drawn, and the tray sits bottom-right over the terminal wall (511-514). The notice at 480 says only "Exception approved once/for this session" and does not name the request. A mis-click approval needs a click at the bottom-right of the right-most pane, within a frame or two of an unpredictable async arrival (held event, then request.get). The key row sits at the bottom of a 420px card, and during SlideUp only part of the card is visible. An agent cannot aim this at the user's pointer, and the keyboard cannot approve because the prompt takes no focus. The risk is real but small, and this is defense-in-depth hardening rather than a demonstrated bypass.

**Also at:** `apps/relay-native/src/guardrail_pages.rs:445`, `apps/relay-native/src/guardrail_pages.rs:480`, `apps/relay-native/src/guardrail_pages.rs:605`

<a id="ra-557"></a>

#### RA-557 · Reset and Save stay live while another scope's layers load, so a reset can clear a field at the wrong scope

`apps/relay-native/src/guardrail_settings.rs:305` · **low** · Bug · plausible · effort S

**Problem.** load() switches to the new `scope` but disables only the inputs (`row.input_widget_sensitive(false)`, 305-307). It keeps `layers` from the previous scope, and the Reset buttons stay visible and clickable. The reset handler compares the old layers' source with the new scope's layer name (590-592) and sets `cleared`, which makes patch() send `null` for that path (334-336). If the load fails (323-325), this state persists indefinitely.

**Impact.** After switching from project A to project B while the load is slow or failed, pressing a Reset left over from A's view and then Save clears B's override for that field. The user never saw that change.

**Fix.** At the start of load, set `layers` to Null so that dirty() is 0, hide the Reset keys, and disable Save and Discard until the new answer arrives. Keep the form disabled if the load fails.

**Verifier note.** Nearly all the risk is in a failed load after a successful one; the in-flight race is milliseconds. A minimal fix: at the start of load(), set layers to Null and call refresh(), which hides the Reset keys and disables Save and Discard. Leave them that way if the load fails.

**Why only plausible.** The mechanism is real. load() (guardrail_settings.rs:297-327) disables only the inputs and keeps the previous scope's `layers`. The reset handler (around 587-597) compares `layers["sources"]` with the new scope's layer name, and project A and project B share the same name ('project'), so it sets `cleared`. patch() (330-352) then sends null for that path to the new scope. However, a successful load runs fill(), which resets every `cleared` flag and refills the inputs (237-246), so in the normal case a stray Reset is wiped out. The bad outcome needs one of two things. Either the user clicks Reset and then Save within the in-flight window of one local guardrail.config.layers call, or that one read fails while the engine still accepts guardrail.config.set. The 'old engine' error at 323-325 does not produce it, because then layers was never loaded and stays Null, so `here` is false. A transient failure on the switch, or a store mutex held by slow handlers that stretches the window, is needed, and I could not establish how likely that is.

**Also at:** `apps/relay-native/src/guardrail_settings.rs:587`, `apps/relay-native/src/guardrail_settings.rs:330`

<a id="ra-558"></a>

#### RA-558 · An agent's starting task is the first ticked card in board-column order, not the task the launch was opened from

`apps/relay-native/src/launch.rs:804` · **low** · Bug · plausible · effort S

**Problem.** `selected_tasks` returns ids in `tasks` insertion order (325-332). That is task.list's column order (`ORDER BY CASE col WHEN 'backlog' THEN 0 WHEN 'in_review' THEN 1 WHEN 'ready' THEN 2 WHEN 'active' THEN 3`, task.rs:855). `tasks.first()` becomes the session's `task_id` (804), and dispatch order sets the queue order (810). The task the sheet was opened from is only preselected (666).

**Impact.** Example: the user opens New session from Ready task #12 (preselected) and also ticks backlog task #3. The agent is created on #3 as its current task and only reaches #12 second.

**Fix.** Keep the preselected task first, then the tasks in the order the user ticked them (record a click sequence), or let the user reorder the queue.

**Verifier note.** This is a UX ordering issue, not a correctness defect. A cheap fix: put the preselected task first in `selected_tasks` for profile 0, or order by tick sequence.

**Why only plausible.** The mechanism is as described. `selected_tasks` (325-332) returns ids in `tasks` push order. That order follows task.list's default sort, `CASE col WHEN 'backlog' THEN 0 WHEN 'in_review' THEN 1 WHEN 'ready' THEN 2 WHEN 'active' THEN 3` (task.rs:855). `tasks.first()` becomes the create's task_id (804), and dispatch order sets queue_ord through assign_session (task.rs:589-600). The task the sheet was opened from is only preselected (666). Nothing documents that the opening task should go first, though. The queue order matches the card order the user sees on the sheet, so this is a UX expectation, not a broken contract. A backlog task outranking a Ready task in the queue is surprising, but the behaviour is deterministic and visible.

**Also at:** `apps/relay-native/src/launch.rs:325`, `apps/relay-native/src/launch.rs:666`, `crates/relay-core/src/handlers/task.rs:855`

<a id="ra-559"></a>

#### RA-559 · Opening a task detail runs four heavy queries, two in sequence, and repeats all of them after every action

`apps/relay-native/src/task_pages.rs:521` · **low** · Performance · plausible · effort M

**Problem.** open() awaits task.get, then module.list, then task.list, one after another (514-524). compose() runs the same pair in parallel with tokio::join! (430-433). task.list returns every task in the project. row_task runs about 10 subqueries per row: sessions, commits, attachments, labels, three relation queries, children, a subtree walk and depth_of (task.rs:229-341). All of it runs under the store mutex (`e.register::<List>`, task.rs:831). It is used only to fill two combos and the child list (714, 754, 807). detail() then calls task.activity straight away (1134). Its audit query applies json_extract to the project's audit rows, newest first, until it has 101 matches (task.rs:760-768). That happens even if Messages and History are never opened. A successful action() closes the detail and calls open() again (1169-1175).

**Impact.** On a project with hundreds of tasks and a long audit history, each detail open holds the single store mutex for a full task.list and an audit scan. Each label add/remove, Move or Link reopens the detail and pays it again. Hooks, guardrail checks and other requests wait behind it, and the detail itself is slow to appear.

**Fix.** Run the calls with tokio::join!. Take the child list from task["children"] or task.children. Fill the parent/relation combos from the board's already-fetched list, or lazily. Load task.activity the first time its tab is shown. After an auxiliary action, refetch task.get only.

**Verifier note.** Child ids already come back in task['children'], and the board has the list already. Parallelize the calls, defer task.activity until its tab is shown, and avoid the full reopen after small actions. The sequential awaits add latency to the panel opening; they do not add mutex hold time.

**Why only plausible.** The call pattern is as described. open() awaits task.get, module.list and task.list one after another (514-524), while compose uses tokio::join!. The full task.list (row_task runs about 10 prepare_cached subqueries per row, under the store mutex via e.register) is used only for the child list, the parent combo and the relation combo. task_activity (960, 1056) runs eagerly, and its audit query scans the project's retained audit rows with json_extract until it has limit+1 matches. For a task with few events that means the whole retained window. action() reopens after each success and also calls refresh_page, so the board runs task.list again. What I could not establish is the real cost. row_task is already optimized (the PERF §1.2 comment), task.list is the same query a board refresh runs anyway, and the audit is pruned by retention. No measurement shows this holding the mutex long enough to be felt. The redundancy is real; the impact is not shown.

**Also at:** `apps/relay-native/src/task_pages.rs:1134`, `apps/relay-native/src/task_pages.rs:1173`, `crates/relay-core/src/handlers/task.rs:229`, `crates/relay-core/src/handlers/task.rs:757`

<a id="ra-560"></a>

#### RA-560 · open() shows late or duplicate task details and misleading ones when list calls fail

`apps/relay-native/src/task_pages.rs:525` · **low** · Bug · plausible · effort M

**Problem.** open() starts a future that awaits three round trips and then always calls `detail(&ui, task, …)` (525). That presents a modal page panel on `ui.page_overlay`, which wraps every page including the agents wall (app.rs:542-544), and makes that page insensitive (panel.rs:244-247). After the awaits there is no project, page or serial check, and there is no guard against an open already in flight. Errors from module.list and task.list become `Value::Null` (520, 524).

**Impact.** When the engine is busy, the detail pops up seconds later over whatever page the user moved to, and disables it. Opening the same card twice (e.g. Enter pressed twice) stacks two editable detail panels whose saves conflict with each other. If task.list fails, the task shows no subtasks and an unselected parent combo; pressing "Set parent" then sends parent_id:null (773) and detaches the task.

**Fix.** Record project, page and a per-open serial before awaiting, and drop the result if they changed. Keep the set of open task ids and present the existing panel instead of making another. Show list errors in the detail status.

**Verifier note.** Severity stays low. Stale or late presentation needs a slow engine (seconds). The parent-null case needs task.list to fail and the user to press Set parent. Fix as suggested: check the page or project after the awaits, de-duplicate by task id, and show list errors.

**Why only plausible.** open() (513-529) has no in-flight or staleness guard. It awaits three calls and then always runs detail(), which makes a Panel::page on ui.page_overlay and presents it, making the host content insensitive (panel.rs:244-252). There is no project, page or serial check. dismiss_panels on navigation only closes panels that already exist, so a late result still appears over the new page. The window is small in practice: the calls are local IPC and normally take milliseconds, and once a detail is presented the board beneath it is insensitive, so a duplicate needs two activations within that window. A stacked duplicate save is caught by the expected/draft_conflicts check, not lost. The parent-detach claim holds as stated. If task.list fails, the parent combo has only the '' row, chosen() returns '', and 'Set parent' sends parent_id:null (773). But that needs a task.list failure followed by a deliberate click.

**Also at:** `apps/relay-native/src/task_pages.rs:520`, `apps/relay-native/src/task_pages.rs:773`, `apps/relay-native/src/panel.rs:244`

<a id="ra-561"></a>

#### RA-561 · The launcher's readiness check treats a busy engine as absent and starts a duplicate that cannot open the store

`run.sh:26` · **low** · Bug · plausible · effort S

**Problem.** `ready() { timeout 2 "$relay" --instance "$RELAY_INSTANCE" ping >/dev/null 2>&1; }`. bus.ping is registered with `e.register` (crates/relay-core/src/handlers/bus.rs:14), so it waits for the store mutex like any handler. If ping takes more than 2 s, line 28 starts a second `serve`. That process cannot open the store, which the live engine holds in locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE (store.rs:394-400), and exits with 'database is locked'. The loop at 35-39 then sees `kill -0` fail, prints 'Relay engine did not become ready' with the duplicate's error as the log tail, and exits 1. `timeout` exits 124 for 'connected but slow' and `relay ping` exits 5 when nothing listens (main.rs:104), but run.sh treats both the same.

**Impact.** Launching while the engine is slow for a few seconds (the condition CLAUDE.md warns about) fails to open the window, blames engine startup, and spawns a stray serve process each time.

**Fix.** Capture ping's exit status. Spawn only on 5 (no engine). On 124, keep polling until the deadline and then report 'engine is running but not answering'. Optionally, check the instance lock (`flock -n .../relay-v4/$RELAY_INSTANCE.lock true`) before spawning.

**Verifier note.** The consequence is a failed launch with a misleading message, followed by a retry. No stray process is left behind, because the duplicate exits on its own, so 'spawns a stray serve process each time' overstates it. The fix is right: tell exit 124 (slow) apart from 5 (unreachable), or check the instance flock before spawning. Registering bus.ping with register_unlocked would also remove the dependence on the mutex.

**Why only plausible.** run.sh:26 checks readiness with `timeout 2 relay ... ping`. bus.ping is registered with e.register (handlers/bus.rs:14), so it waits for the store mutex. If any locked handler holds the mutex for more than about 2 s (including CLI startup and connect), ready() fails and run.sh:32 spawns a second `serve`. serve::start opens the store (serve.rs:21) before it takes the socket flock (socket.rs:68). The duplicate therefore blocks on the EXCLUSIVE store for up to busy_timeout 5000 ms (store.rs:398-400) and exits with an error. kill -0 fails, run.sh prints 'Relay engine did not become ready' with the duplicate's error and exits 1, and the window does not open. The duplicate cannot damage the store, because it never acquires it. I could not show that a 2 s mutex hold happens in normal use at launch. The trigger depends on a slow locked handler, which CLAUDE.md treats as a bug in itself.

**Also at:** `run.sh:28-42`, `crates/relay-core/src/handlers/bus.rs:14-20`, `crates/relay-core/src/store.rs:394-400`, `crates/relay-cli/src/main.rs:104`

#### RA-562 · The fail-closed hook adapters (Claude/Codex PreToolUse translation, Edit/MultiEdit reconstruction, path relativization) have no tests

`crates/relay-cli/src/main.rs:393` · **medium** · Test quality · confirmed · effort M

**Problem.** main.rs has no #[test] at all. relay-cli has no tests directory and nothing uses CARGO_BIN_EXE. crates/relay-core/tests/guardrails.rs only checks that the installed command strings contain "hook claude-report" / "hook codex-pre-tool" (lines 437, 507-509). Everything in main.rs:393-581 is exercised only by hand.

**Impact.** Whether every Claude/Codex write and command is gated depends on this code, and it can regress silently. Several defects in this audit sit in it untested: the missing deadline, the Codex exec mapping, and Edit semantics.

**Fix.** Factor out a pure `gate_payload(tool, tool_input, session, worktree) -> Result<Value>`. Unit-test it with real hook JSON samples: Write, Edit with replace_all, MultiEdit order, missing fields, paths inside and outside the worktree, `..`, apply_patch. Add an integration test that runs the hook binary against `relay serve --instance test` and checks exit codes 0 and 2.

**Verifier note.** The Edit-semantics defect it cites is low and only plausible (cli-main#17). The point stands because of the apply_patch mapping and the fail-open timeout. Factoring a pure `gate_payload(tool, tool_input, input, worktree)` and unit-testing it is the right shape, and it needs no engine. An integration test against `relay serve --instance test` is optional extra coverage.

#### RA-563 · Blender scripts re-implement the mesh and skinning checks per script, and the copies already disagree

`crates/relay-cli/src/blender_py/rig_check.py:106` · **medium** · Duplication · confirmed · effort M

**Problem.** rig_check.py:106-121 repeats mesh_report's bmesh checks (common.py:146-181), on the original rather than evaluated mesh, with opposite severities. A missing UV map is a problem in rig_check (line 107) but a warning in mesh_report (175-176). Zero-area faces are a warning in rig_check (118-119) but a problem in mesh_report, which makes blender_export refuse (165-166). 'Meshes skinned to the armature' is defined three different ways: export.py:20-22 (Armature modifier only), rig_check.py:64 (modifier or parent_type ARMATURE) and render.py:15 (any child, including bone-parented props, or the modifier). rig_check.py:28 computes `deform_roots` and never uses it.

**Impact.** A mesh can pass blender_rig_check and then be refused by blender_export for degenerate faces, or fail the rig check for a missing UV map that export accepts. A body parented with the legacy ARMATURE parent type passes the rig check but is left out of the skeletal FBX.

**Fix.** Have rig_check call mesh_report(o) and add only the skin-specific checks on top. Add one `skinned_meshes(arm)` helper in common.py and use it in export, rig_check and render.

**Verifier note.** Two qualifications. First, render.py:15 including bone-parented props is arguably intended, since a render should show held items. export.py:13-15 deliberately excludes such props with a comment. So the shared skinned_meshes(arm) helper should cover the modifier and parent_type ARMATURE cases for export and rig_check, and render can add children on top. Second, if rig_check reuses mesh_report, the evaluated mesh carries the current pose's deformation. That is acceptable for these checks, but the call has to keep rig_check's weight and influence checks on o.data. The legacy-parent export omission is a real but rare case, since modern Ctrl+P creates a modifier.

#### RA-564 · The Blender and Unreal animation checks are parallel copies that have diverged

`crates/relay-cli/src/unreal_py/common.py:143` · **medium** · Duplication · confirmed · effort L

**Problem.** Left/right naming: blender_py/common.py:42 PAIRS includes '-L'/'-R' and tries prefixes only after every suffix; unreal_py/common.py:143 LEFT_RIGHT has no '-L'/'-R' and interleaves the prefix checks. Segment filters: Blender's SKIP (anim_inspect.py:21-22) has 'ik', 'pole', 'ctrl', 'mch', 'org'; Unreal's SKIP_SEGMENT (common.py:280-281) has 'ik_', 'attach', 'socket', 'camera', 'correct', '_end', 'tip'. Partner probes: Blender adds 'forearm' and 'shin'. Ground: Blender uses the minimum over all bone heads and tails; Unreal uses only foot, ball and toe bones. D161 says both sides use 'the same character frame', so that a problem 'is caught before export and measured again after import'.

**Impact.** The same rig and clip can pass in one tool and fail in the other. For example, a rig named with -L/-R gets pairs and a facing in Blender but falls back to the default frame in Unreal. So the before/after comparison D161 promises is not like-for-like, and every fix has to be made twice: the grip, ground and contact bugs above all exist in both copies.

**Fix.** Move the host-independent logic (pair naming, segment and probe filters, contact, partner and ground checks on plain tuples) into one shared Python file that both blender.rs and unreal.rs include ahead of the host script. Keep only pose sampling host-specific.

**Verifier note.** Sharing is feasible: Blender uses mathutils Vectors and Unreal uses tuples, so the shared module has to run on plain tuples. A pragmatic first step that removes most of the drift is to share only the name tables and the twin/mirror function, the SKIP and probe lists, and the ground rule, as one Python snippet that both blender.rs and unreal.rs prepend (both already concatenate a common script).

**Also at:** `crates/relay-cli/src/blender_py/common.py:42`, `crates/relay-cli/src/blender_py/anim_inspect.py:21`, `crates/relay-cli/src/unreal_py/common.py:280`, `crates/relay-cli/src/blender_py/anim_inspect.py:144`, `crates/relay-cli/src/unreal_py/anim_inspect.py:165`

#### RA-565 · BUS.md §6-§7 and §14 still describe the Tauri app: wrong socket path, UI-executor and door semantics, and 'no RPC over the network'

`docs/engine/BUS.md:323` · **medium** · Docs drift · confirmed · effort S

**Problem.** BUS.md:323-325 gives the socket as `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/relay/<instance>.sock` with bundle ids com.quietsoftware.relay; the code uses `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/relay-v4/` (paths.rs:66-81, whose own doc cites §6.2), and README.md:26-29 notes the old location belongs to the separate Relay-2/V3 engine. §6.1 (311-319) documents a Tauri invoke door; §6.5 (361-372) says ui.* are forwarded to the UI and return unavailable/ui.absent when headless, but handlers/ui.rs:41-66 and 320-363 answer them in core from an in-memory UiRuntime and succeed with no UI; §7 (381) says mirror is 'Tauri Channel only; socket door returns unavailable' while socket.rs streams it; §7 (383) promises a `log` stream from app.log.tail, whose handler only emits `app.log.attached` (handlers/app.rs:133-136); §14 (1121) 'No RPC over the network. Unix socket only' and §4.2 (207-208) 'user needs no token (same uid, same trust)' predate the phone door that forwards user-actor lines from LAN/rendezvous (ARCHITECTURE.md:57-64). SOURCES.md:48 calls docs/engine a preserved Relay-2 reference, yet CLAUDE.md and code comments cite it as current.

**Impact.** A client or script written from §6.2 connects to `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/relay/dev.sock` - the Relay-2/V3 engine's socket if one is running - and silently operates on the wrong store; agents calling ui.toast/ui.page.switch headless get success instead of ui.absent; anyone adding a user-only op reasons from a 'local, same uid' threat model the phone door has invalidated.

**Fix.** Update §6/§7/§14 to the V4 doors (relay-v4 socket path, native client over the socket, core-held UI state, the remote door as a networked user door), or mark them historical and point to ARCHITECTURE.md/MOBILE.md.

**Verifier note.** The SOURCES.md reference is line 19 ('`docs/engine/` preserves Relay-2's bus/spec/decision reference'), not 48. The wrong-store scenario needs a Relay-2/V3 engine to be running, so it is less likely than the stale-threat-model cost. Fix: update §4.2/§6/§7/§14 for the V4 doors and the networked user door (BUS.md:207-208 especially), or mark those sections historical and point to ARCHITECTURE.md and MOBILE.md.

#### RA-566 · BUS.md §9.3/§14 promise a post-hoc `guardrail.violation` watcher with one-click restore for Codex writes; no such detection exists

`docs/engine/BUS.md:529` · **medium** · Docs drift · confirmed · effort S

**Problem.** BUS.md:524-533: 'writes are detected post-hoc by the notify watcher - a destructive write that already landed raises a guardrail.violation notification with a one-click git checkout -- <path> restore (file.restore_head)'; BUS.md:852 and crates/relay-bus/src/ops/file.rs:33 describe file.restore_head as 'the one-click answer to a post-hoc violation'; BUS.md:1130-1131 and D5 (DECISIONS.md:19-21) repeat 'Codex writes are post-hoc'; BUS.md:524-526 and 1056-1057 also say ProviderInfo.guarded is false for Codex. `guardrail.violation` occurs nowhere in the code; the watcher (watch.rs:115-129) only debounces and emits file.changed; providers.rs:212 returns guarded=true for Codex.

**Impact.** A reader trusting the API document believes destructive Codex writes are at least flagged after the fact with a restore button; combined with the exec-only Codex gating, a Codex truncation produces no hold, no refusal and no notification. Developers may also skip real enforcement believing the net exists.

**Fix.** Rewrite §9.3, §14 and the §11.4 guarded comment to D132's hook model and the actual exec-only coverage, or implement the watcher-based violation notification the doc describes.

**Verifier note.** The finding's 'exec-only Codex gating' needs a correction. Codex write tools are hooked (hooks.rs:517). However, codex_pre_tool (relay-cli/src/main.rs:507-512) maps Bash, apply_patch, Edit and Write all to `kind: "exec"`, passing the patch or command text as `command`. guardrail.rs:469-471 then sends them to evaluate_exec, not evaluate_write. As a result, write-path rules (protected paths, destructive-write shape gates) never apply to Codex edits, and the git pre-commit gate is the only write-set enforcement. That is the concrete reason the stale doc matters, and it may deserve its own security or invariant finding. Doc fix: rewrite §9.3, §11.4 and §14, and D5's Codex clause, to match D132. State that Codex edits are gated as exec commands, not as writes, and either remove the 'post-hoc guardrail.violation' wording from the file.restore_head descriptions or build the watcher.

#### RA-567 · session.done never applies the per-task caps BUS.md §9.2 says it enforces, and agents may run git commit --no-verify, so over-cap work reaches review unchecked

`crates/relay-core/src/handlers/session.rs:1140` · **medium** · Docs drift · confirmed · effort M

**Problem.** BUS.md:497 (§9.2) lists `session.done` as an enforcement point: "per-task caps (files, lines) | gate {kind: commit}, git.commit, session.done | refused / guardrail.cap". SPEC.md:134-138 requires per-task caps "enforced in core, never prose". The Done handler (session.rs:1140-1226) contains no guardrail or caps evaluation, and `git log -S guardrail.cap -- session.rs` shows it never had one. At commit time the only enforcement is Relay's pre-commit hook (hooks.rs:116-132), which `git commit --no-verify` skips. `evaluate_exec` (guardrail.rs:811-847) checks only self_approval and `denied_commands`, whose default is ["rm -rf","git reset --hard","git clean -fd","git push --force"] (settings.rs:33). The engine tests call session.done many times (agent_features.rs:207-260, awareness.rs:391-484, phase7.rs:305-313) and none checks caps.

**Impact.** Suppose the pre-commit hook refuses an agent's commit with guardrail.cap, or the agent simply skips hooks. The agent can run `git commit --no-verify` (or `git -c core.hooksPath=/dev/null commit`) and then `session.done`. The task moves to in_review with no refusal, hold or notification, silently bypassing a guardrail the spec says core enforces. I could not establish whether the §9.2 row was meant as a hard guarantee or is aspirational.

**Fix.** Either implement the documented check and add a test: stage session.done, diff the session worktree against its base in prepare, evaluate GateKind::Commit caps in finish, refuse guardrail.cap for agents and hold for the user. Or remove session.done from §9.2 and close the hook bypass in the exec gate by treating `commit --no-verify` / `-n` and `-c core.hooksPath=` as denied for agents.

**Verifier note.** The impact is narrower than 'security high'. The trigger needs an agent that deliberately skips hooks after a cap refusal. The over-cap work is not merged; it lands in in_review, where the user sees the diff. Caps exist to keep review sizes small, and a guardrail.rs comment itself calls agent-side gating best effort ('closes the obvious door, not every door'). The root problem is a documented enforcement point that was never implemented, plus a known hook bypass not in the default exec denials. Rate medium. Fix: either implement the cap check in session.done (staged: diff against base in prepare, evaluate in finish) or correct §9.2, and add the hook-skipping git forms to the agent exec denials.

#### RA-568 · session.discard_restorable copies session.close's cleanup and has already drifted from it, leaving guardrail holds open forever

`crates/relay-core/src/handlers/session.rs:1526` · **medium** · Duplication · confirmed · effort S

**Problem.** DiscardRestorable's finish (1526-1541) re-implements Close's finish (1598-1638) but leaves out `UPDATE holds SET state='expired' ... WHERE session_id=? AND state='open'` (1612-1616), the device-lease release, and branch_cleanup::after_close (1630-1636). Its prepare also leaves out remove_hook_dir (1596) and always purges build output.

**Impact.** Declining resume for a session that had a pending guardrail hold (e.g. a held destructive write when the app closed) leaves the hold 'open' forever. It stays on the dashboard (notify.rs:168), and guardrail.confirm on a gate hold fails because `sessions::by_name` can no longer find the closed session (handlers/guardrail.rs:600). Branch cleanup waits for the 20-minute sweep and hook dirs wait for the next startup sweep. Every future fix to close cleanup has to be made twice.

**Fix.** Move the row cleanup into one helper, e.g. `close_row(ctx, s)`, and use it from both ops; or implement discard as Close with remove_worktree:true after the restorable check.

**Verifier note.** Two corrections to the impact. First, the hold is not stuck 'forever': guardrail.reject (guardrail.rs:708-723) works without the session row, so the user can clear it by hand. Second, the device-lease release is moot, because leases are held in engine memory (engine.rs:431) and a restorable session only exists after a restart. The real gaps are the open holds, branch cleanup waiting for the periodic sweep, and the hook dir waiting for the next startup sweep. Fix: factor the closed-row cleanup (state, claims, pair_with, scrollback, holds expiry, events, after_commit branch cleanup) into one helper shared by Close and DiscardRestorable, and call remove_hook_dir in the discard prepare.
